title: Abu Talib's house
hookLine: his uncle, poor and with many children, raises him as his own

lines: A CROWDED HOUSE, A THIN PURSE.
cards: One more grave. The old man who spread his rug by the Ka'ba dies too, the sirah says, while the boy is still young. Before he goes, Abd al-Muttalib asks one of his sons to take the orphan in.
He chooses Abu Talib, the full brother of the boy's father, Abdullah, born of the same mother. And Abu Talib's house is already crowded, and his purse is thin. Today: Abu Talib.

teach.b: The sirah describes Abu Talib as a man of little money and a full house. Taking the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in means one more mouth at a table that's already stretched.
He takes him anyway, and the sirah remembers his love for the boy.
Ibn Ishaq says Abu Talib kept the boy close, and would take him along where he went. Notice the shape of this. The boy has lost a father he never saw, a mother on the road, and now a grandfather.
Each time, someone stands in the gap. Halimah, who took the baby nobody wanted. Umm Ayman, who carried him home from Abwa.
Abd al-Muttalib, on the rug. Now an uncle who can't really afford it. The Qur'an later speaks to the Prophet about exactly this.
In surah ninety-three it reminds him that he was an orphan who was sheltered, and then it draws the line from his past to his duty.
Pickthall translates: "Therefore the orphan oppress not." What was done for him, he is to do for others. And the story comes full circle in his own life.

Years later, Ibn Ishaq says, when hard times fell on Quraysh and Abu Talib's family was struggling, Muhammad went to his uncle al-Abbas and proposed that each of them take one of Abu Talib's sons to ease the load.
Muhammad took Ali, and raised him in his own home.
The boy who was given room became the man who made room.

how: Muslims remember Abu Talib as the uncle who raised and protected the Prophet ﷺ, and care for orphans is taught from surah 93 and from the Prophet's own childhood.

o: the uncle who took the orphaned boy into his home
the Prophet's elder brother, who raised him
the grandfather who sat him on the rug

games.q: Abu Talib's house — tap the pairs.
p: full brother of the boy's father
entrusted the boy before he died

s: Abu Talib was the richest of the uncles
the sirah describes him as a man of little money and a full house.
later, Muhammad took in Abu Talib's son Ali
Ibn Ishaq says it was to ease his uncle's load in hard times.
surah ninety-three ties his orphanhood to care for orphans

games.q: you're Abu Talib. money is short and your house is full. your dying father asks you to raise your brother's orphaned son. what do you do?
o: take him in and keep him close.
send him back to Halimah's tribe.
games.why: he took him in, the sirah says, loved him and kept him close; years later Muhammad did the same for Abu Talib's son Ali.

practice: Who made room for you when it cost them something: a relative who took you in, a teacher who stayed late, a friend who shared a small apartment?
Let one person come clearly to mind, the table or the couch or the car, and say thank you to them in your heart, plainly, as if they were sitting across from you.
If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward them; if not, just let the thanks be full.

wordCard.voice: Abu Talib. The Prophet's uncle, a man of little money and a full house, who took the orphan in after his grandfather died, and kept him close. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: there was room. Tomorrow, the shepherd in the hills. See you then.

sources.ref: Qur'an 93:6 (found thee an orphan and protected)
